title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 6: Rotarians Defend the Rule of Law
keywords: Rotarians Defend the Rule of Law
9th Conference of Chief Justices of Asia and the Pacific
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- an address to a Rotary District Conference in which CJP grounded his appeal in Rotary's own creed, since the 'ABCs of Rotary' says a world-minded Rotarian defends the rule of law and encourages high ethical standards, making Rotarians natural partners of magistrates.

He updated the Rotarians on the 'Davide Watch,' the reform program begun when Hilario G. Davide Jr. took his oath as Chief Justice on November 30, 1998, insisting it was not a collection of motherhood statements but a definite development plan carried out daily through the Action Program for Judicial Reforms and monitored by a full-time Program Management Office.

He selected four reform projects in which Rotarians might especially assist -- the Zero Backlog program, court computerization and construction, the education program for judges and lawyers, and Alternative Dispute Resolution -- out of more than fifty reform projects then under way.

He reported the international acclaim the program had won at the 9th Conference of Chief Justices of Asia and the Pacific in Christchurch and closed by inviting Rotarians and Rotary clubs to lend a hand so that the Court could deliver the speedy quality justice Filipinos deserve.
sub_topics: Why Supreme Court justices keep a low profile: the nature of their work means acting quietly on matters officially brought by litigants, and he had explained this at the same district conference in March 2000.

His own Rotary record -- perfect attendance for 12 years from 1983 to 1995 -- broken by a judicial workload requiring long days and nights seven days a week, which forced him to decline many speaking invitations.

The persistence of District Governor Rudy Estrellado and Conference Chairman Boy Villareal, who sent club president Ed Tumangan to his chambers, and Tumangan's suggestion that he speak on judicial reform so Rotarians might extend support.

The Rotary warrant for the topic: Cliff Dochterman's 'ABCs of Rotary' defines Rotary as business and professional persons who encourage high ethical standards, and says a world-minded Rotarian defends the rule of law and order to preserve individual liberty.

The 'Davide Watch' vision of an independent, effective and efficient judiciary worthy of public trust and a legal profession providing quality, ethical, accessible and cost-effective legal service, backed by the Philippine government, local donors, UNDP, the World Bank, the Asia Foundation, UNICEF, the ADB and bilateral assistance from the European Union, Japan, Canada, Australia, the United States and the Netherlands.

Unprecedented discipline as proof of commitment: for the first time in 100 years the Court censured one of its own members, dismissed a Court of Appeals justice and suspended the Sandiganbayan presiding magistrate, besides removing, suspending and fining many lower court judges for misconduct, dishonesty, immorality, incompetence and unreasonable delay.

The centenary frame: more than 50 reform projects highlighted during the celebrations superintended by the Centenary Executive Committee he chairs, with the Court's exact 100th birthday on June 11, 2001 and the celebrations extended to June 11 of the current year.

The breadth of the reforms, from law school curricula, bar examinations, aid to poor law students and professorial chairs, through rigid screening of appointees, strict ethics enforcement, continuing legal education and performance monitoring.

Compensation as the converse of expectation: exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and a lump-sum budget the Court may itself break into line items, so judges' pay can be raised by realignment without additional funding.

Zero Backlog: the Constitution's decision periods of 24 months for the Supreme Court, 12 for the Court of Appeals and 3 for lower courts, counted from the filing of the last pleading -- and the Court's reduction of dormant cases from about 2,000 in 1995 to fewer than 50.

The Court of Appeals' own backlog program under Presiding Justice Alicia Austria-Martinez, expected to clear its long-idle cases in two years, and Court Administrator Presbitero J. Velasco Jr.'s strategy for the trial courts.

The lower-court arithmetic from his 2000 book 'Transparency, Unanimity & Diversity': for 1995-1999, RTC filings outstripped decisions by about 6,800 a year, and in the first-level courts case inflow exceeded outflow by almost 65,000 a year.

Computerization: 1,500 personal computers purchased for courts nationwide loaded with Lex Libris containing Supreme Court decisions from 1901, the judiciary's homepage www.supremecourt.gov.ph, computerized internal processes and case tracking, and the prospect of monitoring all trial court calendars from Manila terminals.
Sen. Aquilino Pimentel Jr.'s initiative for pilot 'e-courts' in Metro Manila and Cebu with computer-aided transcription, video equipment, websites and cyberspace linkup.

Courthouse construction: squalid and humid salas replaced by fast-tracked Halls of Justice, with Manila's still under construction on the former Jai-Alai building site on Taft Avenue, and the year 2010 envisioned for paperless courts as pioneered by Singapore and Australia.

The education program: updated Rules of Court and all-new rules on electronic evidence, corporate rehabilitation, intra-corporate controversies, family disputes, intellectual property infringement and juveniles in conflict with the law; plus live-in seminars on deregulation, privatization, trade liberalization, biotechnology, DNA, cloning and stem cells.
Alternative Dispute Resolution: Filipinos' litigiousness and clogged dockets answered by negotiation, arbitration and mediation, especially where litigants must keep good relations afterward.

The mediation results: about 400 mediators trained by the Philippine Judicial Academy and put to work in March-April 2001 on cases in the National Capital Region, Cebu and Davao, settling more than 80 percent of the 1,000 cases referred, some of which had dragged on over 10 years.

Christchurch, October 4-8, 2001: attending the 9th Conference of Chief Justices of Asia and the Pacific for the indisposed Chief Justice Davide, he heard UN special rapporteur Dato Param Cumaraswamy praise the Philippine judiciary's reform and independence and World Bank executive Anthony Toft commend the 'Davide Watch' to international donors.

stances.claim: Rotary and the judiciary share a vocation: because the 'ABCs of Rotary' commits Rotarians to encouraging high ethical standards and to defending the rule of law and order to preserve individual liberty, Rotarians are the judiciary's natural allies in judicial reform.
stances.rhetorical_move: appeal from the audience's own charter: quoting Rotary's founding definitions back to Rotarians to convert an update into an invitation

stances.claim: The 'Davide Watch' is not merely a broad collection of motherhood statements and principles but a definite development plan implemented day after day through the APJR, monitored by a full-time Program Management Office and backed by named domestic and international donors.
stances.rhetorical_move: plan-versus-rhetoric distinction, substantiated by naming the monitoring office and the donor roster

stances.claim: If the judiciary expects to recruit and keep the best and the brightest, it must compensate them properly -- 'from whom much is expected, so also should much be given' -- through exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and a lump-sum budget the Court itself may allocate.
stances.rhetorical_move: inversion of a familiar maxim into a reciprocal obligation, then translated into two concrete legislative asks

stances.claim: Filipinos' litigiousness clogs the dockets, and negotiation, arbitration and mediation should be used instead of full-blown litigation, especially where the parties are relatives or neighbors or where commercial relations must survive the dispute.
stances.rhetorical_move: cultural diagnosis followed by pilot evidence -- 400 trained mediators settling more than 80 percent of 1,000 referred cases, some pending over 10 years, within two weeks

stances.claim: The Philippine judicial reform program has earned international acclaim and has become the envy of many countries, as shown by the Christchurch conference where the Philippines was treated as a role model.
stances.rhetorical_move: external-validation argument, sourced to a UN special rapporteur and a World Bank executive rather than to his own assessment

notable_anecdotes: He recalled enjoying perfect Rotary attendance for 12 years, from 1983 to 1995, before the Supreme Court's grueling schedule of long days and nights seven days a week ended his 100 percent presence.

District Governor Rudy Estrellado and Conference Chairman Boy Villareal were so relentless that they sent his club president Ed Tumangan to his chambers in person, and Tumangan reminded him that RI President Richard King -- present at his 2000 address -- wanted an encore.

He noted with a Rotarian's wink that the new court administrator, Justice Presbitero J. Velasco Jr., is himself a Rotarian who has also been unable to maintain his attendance since his appointment -- the consolation being that he is at work solving the delay problem in the lower courts.

He observed that many lawyers, litigants, witnesses and plain citizens have chuckled at unsanitary courtrooms and trials held in small, squalid and humid salas, and pointed out that the City of Manila does not even have its own Hall of Justice, still under construction on the former Jai-Alai building site on Taft Avenue.
He reported that municipal trial courts are not uncommonly loaded with 6,000 cases, mostly collections on bounced checks.

After the Christchurch session on judicial reform, he was literally mobbed by other delegates asking how the Philippines had secured the endorsement of the UN and the World Bank and how they might get assistance from international donors -- leaving him, he said, never more proud of being a Filipino jurist.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced an address to a Rotary District Conference. Justice Panganiban explained that Supreme Court justices keep a low profile and act quietly on matters brought by litigants, and that his workload had ended the perfect Rotary attendance he had enjoyed for 12 years from 1983 to 1995; he accepted the invitation only after District Governor Rudy Estrellado and Conference Chairman Boy Villareal sent his club president Ed Tumangan to his chambers. He justified the topic from Rotary's own creed, quoting Cliff Dochterman's 'ABCs of Rotary' that Rotarians encourage high ethical standards and that a world-minded Rotarian defends the rule of law, and observing that this common passion unites Rotarians with magistrates. He then updated them on the 'Davide Watch' begun when Hilario G. Davide Jr. took his oath on November 30, 1998, insisting it was not a collection of motherhood statements but a plan implemented day after day through the Action Program for Judicial Reforms, monitored by a full-time Program Management Office and supported by the Philippine government, local donors, UNDP, the World Bank, the Asia Foundation, UNICEF, the ADB and several bilateral donors. As proof of commitment he cited the Court's unprecedented discipline of its own, and as proof of reciprocity he asked for exemption from the Salary Standardization Law and a lump-sum budget. He then described four projects Rotarians might assist: Zero Backlog, which had cut the Court's dormant cases from about 2,000 in 1995 to fewer than 50 while lower-court inflow still outran outflow by thousands of cases a year; computerization, with 1,500 computers loaded with Lex Libris, a judiciary homepage, prospective e-courts and new Halls of Justice on the way to paperless courts by 2010; education, with updated Rules of Court, all-new rules on electronic evidence and other novel subjects, and live-in seminars on the new economy and the new biosciences; and Alternative Dispute Resolution, where Philippine Judicial Academy-trained mediators settled more than 80 percent of 1,000 referred cases in 2001. He recounted the Christchurch conference of October 2001, where a UN special rapporteur and a World Bank executive praised the program, and closed by inviting Rotarians to help implement it.
